subject: Onramp options for Redwood Private — quick technical runbook and asks
messages:
From: Asha Shroff <asha@acme-analytics.com>
To: kimberly.park@redwood.com
Cc: netops@acme-analytics.com, ben.carter@redwood.com
Date: Thu, 21 Aug 2025 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Connecting Acme on-prem to Redwood Private — initial asks

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks for taking this. We are evaluating Redwood Private for a pilot and need to decide an ingress path from our on-prem datacenter (Equinix / Cisco stack) into the Redwood VPCs. Our security and netops teams asked for a short comparison of the three common options: VPC Peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints / endpoint services), and site-to-site VPN.

Top constraints for us:
- We can't move account ownership for project resources — peering across accounts is allowed but our security team dislikes long-lived cross-account peering.
- Need predictable egress IPs for allowlisting (for SOC2 evidence).
- Throughput target: sustained 300 Mbps for model payloads, spikes to ~700 Mbps during ingestion windows.
- RTO/RPO for inference of <200ms p95; control-plane ops are less sensitive.

Can you send a concise recommendation that covers: required account-level work, NAT/egress requirements, HA considerations, and a pragmatic path for POC -> production? Attached a short network diagram.

Thanks — please loop anyone on your side who should be aware.

—Asha
Asha Shroff
Head of Platform Engineering, Acme Analytics

Attachment: network-flow-diagram.png (diagram stub)

From: kimberly.park@redwood.com
To: Asha Shroff <asha@acme-analytics.com>
Cc: ben.carter@redwood.com, david.kim@redwood.com
Date: Thu, 21 Aug 2025 11:05:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Connecting Acme on-prem to Redwood Private — initial asks

Hi Asha — thanks, this is exactly the right set of constraints. Quick, pragmatic reply here and then Ben will add the low-level config notes.

High-level tradeoffs (short):
- VPC Peering: simple L3 connectivity and low latency. But it creates a long-lived peering relationship between AWS accounts and requires route management across VPCs. Not ideal if Acme wants strict account isolation or has policy against peering with vendor-managed VPCs. No built-in allowlist for egress IPs — you must use NAT or a proxy in the peered VPC.

- PrivateLink (interface endpoints / endpoint service): preserves account isolation (Acme creates ENIs in their VPC that connect to our endpoint service). Provides a stable endpoint on Acme's side and avoids peering. We can provide a small set of stable ingress IPs if Acme front-ends the endpoint with an NLB under your account, or we can publish a list of NLB IPs (note: NLB IPs can change unless you own the LB). Slightly more operational setup (endpoint service acceptance, NLB config) but cleaner from a security/governance perspective.

- Site-to-site VPN: Fastest to stand up for a POC; supports NAT and egress allowlisting easily because Acme controls the tunnel endpoint. Latency and bandwidth are variable depending on the transit path; for sustained high throughput you'll need multiple tunnels or a managed VPN appliance. Good fallback plan.

Suggested pragmatic path:
1) POC: Stand up an IPsec S2S VPN for 2 weeks to validate throughput and request patterns. This gives immediate allowlisting and minimal cross-account setup.
2) Prod: If account isolation is required, move to PrivateLink (endpoint service) with an Acme-owned NLB in front; provide the PrivateLink service from our side and document acceptance workflow. If you prefer simpler steady-state networking and both sides agree to peer, evaluate VPC Peering only if your security team signs off on the account relationship.

Action items needed from Acme:
- Confirm whether Acme can host an NLB in your account (gives best allowlist guarantees).
- Provide egress IP requirements (CIDR or nat IPs) and bandwidth profile per-hour.
- If you want a VPN POC, share your public VPN endpoints, PSK or certificate preference, and preferred IKE settings.

I'll attach a one-page matrix and a config-snippets file that Ben curated.

—Kimberly
Kimberly Park
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Attachment: privatelink-vs-peering-matrix.xlsx (matrix stub)
Attachment: config-snippets.txt (snippet stub)

From: ben.carter@redwood.com
To: kimberly.park@redwood.com, Asha Shroff <asha@acme-analytics.com>
Cc: david.kim@redwood.com
Date: Fri, 22 Aug 2025 08:47:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Connecting Acme on-prem to Redwood Private — initial asks

Adding low-level notes and an ops checklist. Quoting Asha's original to keep context.

On Thu, 21 Aug 2025 at 09:12 AM Asha Shroff <asha@acme-analytics.com> wrote:
> Top constraints for us:
> - We can't move account ownership for project resources — peering across accounts is allowed but our security team dislikes long-lived cross-account peering.
> - Need predictable egress IPs for allowlisting (for SOC2 evidence).

Technical notes:
- Peering specifics:
  * Cross-account peering requires both accounts to accept the peering request; transitive routing is not supported by default (no peering transit). If Acme is unwilling to add a route into your VPCs pointing to an external vendor VPC, peering is a non-starter.
  * For egress IPs with peering: you must NAT in either side (e.g., Acme NAT GW in their VPC) or build a proxy with elastic IPs. That adds operational overhead.

- PrivateLink specifics:
  * On our side, we configure an endpoint service backed by an NLB (recommended for scale). The NLB sits in our VPC and forwards to the redwood-private instances (or target group).
  * Acme creates an interface endpoint in their VPC which shows up as ENIs with private IPs. From a routing perspective, traffic stays in the Acme VPC until it hits the ENI.
  * If Acme owns the NLB (recommended), Acme can control the egress IPs (ELB static IPs via NLB + Elastic IP per AZ) and provide allowlistable addresses. If Redwood owns the NLB, we can publish the current IPs but they may change (not ideal for SOC2).
  * Endpoint acceptance step: Acme will need to accept our endpoint service (this is a simple console/API step and can be automated via CLI).

- VPN specifics:
  * Quick to provision: two tunnels, BGP optional. Throughput via software tunnels can be limited; for sustained 700 Mbps you should either use a hardware VPN appliance or bundle multiple tunnels and do flow hashing.
  * Egress IPs: trivial to lock down — Acme controls the customer gateway IPs and can NAT to a known set of public IPs.

Operational checklist for a PrivateLink production cutover (recommended if you need account isolation):
- [ ] Acme to provision NLB (or agree to allow Redwood to publish static NLB IPs).
- [ ] Exchange endpoint service names and accept the service on Acme side.
- [ ] Validate MTU (ENI path may add overhead), test with 1GB samples.
- [ ] Run perf test for 48 hours to validate p95 and throughput.
- [ ] Add monitoring (vpc flow logs + endpoint health) and document runbook for cutover rollback back to VPN.

Config snippets included show an example ipsec tunnel, example AWS CLI commands to accept an endpoint, and an NLB healthcheck suggestion (HTTP 200 /health).

Ben Carter
Senior Network Engineer, Redwood Inference

Attachment: config-snippets.txt (shows IKE v2 sample, AWS CLI accept command, NLB target group config)

Kimberly / Ben — thanks, this is very helpful and practical. A few quick replies from netops:
- We can host an NLB in our account and allocate Elastic IPs per AZ (happy to do that for production).
- For the POC we want the fastest path: we will stand up a VPN appliance and share public endpoints + PSK by EOD tomorrow.
- Security wants the endpoint acceptance workflow documented (audit trail) — can Redwood produce an acceptance log or automation snippet that writes to a shareholder bucket?

Proposed short timeline:
1) Tomorrow (26 Aug): Acme provides VPN endpoints and PSK; Redwood provides ipsec sample and we stand up VPN POC.
2) Week of Sep 8: If POC perf is good, Acme provisions NLB + EIPs and we begin PrivateLink acceptance flow.

Can you send a short runbook (2 pages) for the acceptance + monitoring steps we can attach to our SOC2 evidence? If possible include the exact AWS CLI commands for the accept step and an example of the minimal CloudTrail/audit entry we should capture.

Thanks again — looping in netops for visibility.
